EL1-F-01.hint: In an exponential function, equal steps in \(x\) multiply \(y\) by the same number. Divide each output by the one before it and see whether the ratios match.
slips: Checking differences instead of ratios. A constant difference means a linear function.
Checking only one pair of consecutive outputs. Check them all.

EL1-F-02.hint: Replace \(x\) with the input, then apply the exponent before you multiply by the coefficient. A negative exponent means a reciprocal.
slips: Multiplying the coefficient and the base first. In \(3\cdot 2^{4}\), compute \(2^{4}\) first.
Treating a negative exponent as a negative number. \(2^{-3}\) is \(\dfrac{1}{8}\), not \(-8\).

EL1-F-03.hint: The point with \(x=0\) gives \(a\). Put the other point into \(y=ab^{x}\) and solve for \(b\).
slips: Using the \(y\)-value of the second point as \(b\). It is \(ab^{n}\), so you must undo the power.
Forgetting to take the root. If \(b^{3}=64\), then \(b=4\), not \(64\).

EL1-A-01.hint: Part (a): compare ratios. Part (b): exponent before coefficient. Part (c): the point with \(x=0\) gives \(a\) (or divide the two equations if neither point has \(x=0\)).
slips: Using differences in part (a). Exponential functions have a constant ratio.

EL1-A-02.hint: Write one equation for each point, then divide the second equation by the first. The \(a\) cancels and you are left with a power of \(b\).
slips: Subtracting the equations instead of dividing them. Division cancels \(a\); subtraction does not.
Finding \(b\) and stopping. You still need \(a\) from one of the original equations.
